This makes the shuffle automatically split the other dimensions by a dynamic factor so that the maximum chunksize stays the same after the shuffle. The implementation ensures that we only split chunks along the other dimensions so that we can avoid different input chunks having to communicate with each other

cc @dcherian is this roughly what you imagined? We can add the option to customise how we split as a follow up

comments.body: It seems like we could generalize this to things like `reshape` too, so perhaps `array.chunksize-tolerance` instead?

```suggestion
    max_axis_chunks = max(x.chunks[axis])
```

```suggestion
            max_axis_chunks ** (1 / (len(x.chunks) - 1))
```

why the exponential?
Can you use `divmod` here?
don't follow
chunks is currently only string, but I'll add type hints.
That sounds like a good idea, yes. I'll rename the option in another PR
Assuming 3 dimensions and we shuffle on axis=0, I want to allocate the split factor equally to the other dimensions, i.e. if the factor is 4, I want to split axis=1 and axis=2 by half each.
Bad variable naming probably. We are building the new chunk sizes for the axis we are currently investigating.
Oh I always keep forgetting that, yep that's a good point
ah I see . a comment would help. I think the rewrite to `max_axis_chunks` is also useful, otherwise you multiply by `new_max_group` and then divide by `new_max_group`
I need a bit more, but we can definitely simplify these formulas a lot

Yeah I rewrote this, that was actually way to complicate.

I'll add a comment
Why is one `extend` and the other `append`?
When we don’t split up the chunk then c is a single element, if we split c up in multiple new chunks then it’s a list of new chunk sizes that represent the old chunk
Do we redistribute whatever portion of the factor remains onto the other dimensions?
Yeah that's a good point, not currently. I can do that as a follow up

> I can do that as a follow up

Works for me as long as we eventually ensure that there's no "size creep". As a suggestion for that, I'd consider going round-robin and halving the max size each time, skipping len-1 dimensions. This would also get rid of the smart-yet-cumbersome exponential.
